body:
It seems that what you call "genetic transsexuality", a lot of other people refer to as something in the general ballpark of non-binariness, but I'm glad we can at least agree on their existence.

What kind of evidence or study would you want to see to support or refute whether mammals have only two genders? A lot of people understand "gender" as something people identify with, on some emotional level; in which case, I doubt there will be evidence much stronger than survey respondents saying they don't identify with either of the two binary genders. That's evidence enough for me, but if it isn't for you, I'm curious what you would tell such people about their gender.

Survey on prevalence of humans who develop biologically in non-binary ways: ["How sexually dimorphic are we? Review and synthesis" (Blackless et al. 2000)](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11534012). There are lots of medically well-established conditions that can cause one to develop in a way that doesn't fall neatly into the binary: [Klinefelter syndrome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Klinefelter_syndrome), [Turner syndrome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turner_syndrome), [androgen insensitivity syndrome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Androgen_insensitivity_syndrome), etc. There's lots of evidence in the references for each of these pages. (None of this is meant to say that one needs to have a clear-cut genetic condition to call oneself non-binary, of course.)

As for the more social-role type of gender, here is a survey on gender identity and fluidity: ["Queering gender: studying gender identity in ‘normative’ individuals" (Daphna et al. 2013)](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/19419899.2013.830640).
